title: Lesson 8: Marriage and Relationships
description: Marriage is not finding a finished statue. It is two people who see what Jesus is making in each other, hand each other the chisel, and trust God to shape them both. Through a picture from Tim and Kathy Keller, God's covenant with Abram, and Ephesians 5, you will see the covenant love God gives first and why drawing near to God draws two people near to each other.

blocks.text: You have spent this course learning to love outward: your neighbors, your family at home, your church family, and the people your gifts can bless. This lesson looks at the love that holds your closest relationships together. It is called covenant love, and it starts with the way God has already loved you.

blocks.title: The Marble and the Chisel
blocks.text:
In The Meaning of Marriage, Kathy Keller writes, "Most people, when they are looking for a spouse, are looking for a finished statue when they should be looking for a wonderful block of marble. Not so you can create the kind of person you want, but rather because you see what kind of person Jesus is making." Nobody you love is finished, and neither are you. Love begins with the willingness to look at a rough block of stone and see what Jesus is making in it.

Tim Keller adds that marriage exposes the rough edges in your own character. So picture marriage like this: you hand the other person your chisel, and they hand you theirs. You let them see your pride and selfishness, and you trust God to use them to shape you. A chisel in loving hands is patient and careful, and it is never a license to wound. That is what marriage is: two people willing to see something good in each other, pass the chisel, and trust each other with it.

That kind of trust does not come naturally. Most of us protect ourselves and keep score. So where does the courage to hand someone your chisel come from? It starts with the way God has already loved you.
8.1 - When you look at the people closest to you, do you tend to see a finished statue you are measuring or a block of marble Jesus is shaping? What makes it hard for you to hand someone your chisel?
God Went First

blocks.alt: Abram asleep under the stars while a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch pass between shadowed covenant pieces

blocks.text: Long before Jesus, God showed Abram what covenant love looks like. God had promised Abram a family too large to count, but years went by with no child, and Abram asked how he could be sure (Genesis 15:8). So God told him to prepare a covenant. Abram cut a heifer, a goat, and a ram in half and laid the pieces in two rows with a path between them (Genesis 15:9-10). Bible scholars explain that in that time, both people making a covenant could walk between the pieces, as if to say, "May this happen to me if I break my promise" (compare Jeremiah 34:18). But a deep sleep fell on Abram, and in the dark "a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces" (Genesis 15:17). Only God, pictured by the fire, passed through, taking the whole weight of the promise on Himself.

Abram's part was to believe. Keeping the promise was God's part alone. That is what a covenant is: a binding promise. Before covenant love is something you give, it is something you receive. At the cross, Jesus showed how far God's faithful love would go. He paid for your sin, and you can trust Him to keep His promises.
The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
Closer to God, Closer to Each Other

Every close relationship runs on one of two agreements. A contract says, "I will, if you will." It keeps score and lasts only as long as the other person performs. A covenant says, "I will, even when." It rests on a promise, so it holds on the hard days. Tap through the diagram to see where that kind of love comes from.

Two people do not grow close by trying harder. They grow close as each one draws near to God. Just as God alone passed between the pieces while Abram slept, Jesus carried the cost of the covenant Himself. He called His death the "new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). You give covenant love because you have received it.
8.2 - In one close relationship, where are you keeping score: "I will, if you will"? What would "I will, even when" look like there this week?
Marriage: Christ's Love on Display

God designed marriage to be a billboard of covenant love, a living picture of how Christ loves His church. In Ephesians 5, Paul begins with a word for every Christian: "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21). Before anyone talks about roles, everyone bows low before Jesus.

Then Paul speaks to wives: "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:22), and later he asks them to respect their husbands (Ephesians 5:33). Biblical submission is not inferiority, silence, passivity, or following someone into sin. It is honoring and helping a husband under Jesus.
Paul gives his longest words to husbands, and they may be the hardest of all.
Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,

Jesus did not wait for His bride to become lovely before He loved her. He gave Himself for her while she was still wandering. So a husband's leadership is measured by his sacrifice, not his control. If you promised you would die for her, you can lay down your pride for her today: go first in serving, first in saying "I was wrong," and first in giving up your comfort for her good.
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.

Here is the mystery: every Christian marriage is a small picture of Jesus and His church, two imperfect people held by a faithful God. Marriage is a blessing, but only Jesus can be your ultimate satisfaction.

Because two sinners share one home, forgiveness is the oxygen of a Christian marriage. It sounds like, "I was wrong. Will you forgive me?" and "I forgive you." Remember the servant in Jesus' parable who was forgiven an impossible debt and then refused to forgive a small one (Matthew 18:23-35). When you remember how much God has forgiven you, you can stop keeping score. In Christ, people change, and marriages can grow.

blocks.title: What covenant love is not
content: Covenant love is patient with ordinary weakness and ordinary hard days. It is not a promise to stay in danger. Ephesians 5 calls a husband to lay down his life, never to control, threaten, or harm, and biblical submission never means following someone into sin or accepting abuse. God never asks you to cover for someone who is hurting you or your children, and keeping your promises does not make you responsible for another person's sin.

If someone is harming, threatening, or controlling you, please tell a pastor or another safe, trusted person and get help. If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or your local emergency number. In the United States you can also call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

blocks.text: 8.3 - If you are married, where do you need to lay down your pride, ask forgiveness, or serve first this week? If you are not married, where can you practice covenant love in a close friendship or your church family?
Every Season Can Be Faithful

Maybe you are single and hoping to marry, or single and content. Maybe you are divorced, widowed, raising children on your own, or blending two families. Maybe your marriage is hard right now. God does not treat any of these seasons as a waiting room. Jesus Himself never married, and He lived the most complete human life ever lived.

Ephesians 5 is not only for married people. The deepest marriage in the passage is Christ and the church, and if you belong to Jesus, you are part of the bride He gave Himself for. Paul, who was also unmarried, called singleness a gift, not a lesser life.
I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.

Paul even said an unmarried person can have a special freedom for "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The triangle works in every season. Whether you are married, engaged, or dating, as you and the other person each draw near to God, you draw near to each other. Your worth is not measured by your relationship status. There is a faithful way to live in the season you are in right now.
8.4 - What is hardest about the season of life you are in right now? What would faithfulness look like in it this week, instead of waiting for a different season?
Lesson 8 Review

Marriage is not finding a finished statue. It is two people willing to see what Jesus is making in each other, pass the chisel, and trust each other with it. That trust grows out of covenant love. While Abram slept, God alone passed between the pieces. A contract says, "I will, if you will," but a covenant says, "I will, even when." Jesus showed that love completely when He gave Himself up for His church (Ephesians 5:25), and as two people draw near to God, they draw near to each other. In the next lesson, you will see how purity protects these covenant relationships.
